paragraphs.heading: Two kinds of ozone loss
paragraphs.text: Ozone depletion names two linked changes in the stratosphere, home of the ozone layer, seen since the late 1970s. One is a fall in the total amount of ozone in the upper stratosphere. The other is a much bigger loss each spring around the polar regions. Over the south pole, that springtime loss is called the ozone hole. Polar tropospheric ozone depletion events also happen in spring, alongside the stratospheric ones.

paragraphs.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs.text: The ozone layer stops harmful ultraviolet light, called UVB, from getting through the atmosphere. Those wavelengths cause skin cancer, sunburn, cataracts and permanent blindness, and they harm plants and animals too. As the ozone thinned, these harms were projected to rise sharply, which raised worldwide concern. That concern brought about the Montreal Protocol in 1987, a ban on making CFCs, halons and other ozone-depleting chemicals.

paragraphs.heading: What causes it
paragraphs.text: The main culprits are manufactured chemicals, above all halocarbons used as refrigerants, solvents, propellants and foam-blowing agents: CFCs (chlorofluorocarbons), HCFCs and halons. Together these are known as ozone-depleting substances, or ODS. Once released at the surface, they are carried up into the stratosphere by turbulent mixing, faster than they can settle out. There, ultraviolet light breaks them apart, a process called photodissociation, and frees halogen atoms that speed up the conversion of ozone (O₃) into ordinary oxygen (O₂). As halocarbon emissions grew, the measured ozone loss grew with them.

paragraphs.heading: A chain reaction
paragraphs.text: Several free radicals can destroy ozone; a radical has an unpaired electron, which makes it extremely reactive. The most important are hydroxyl (OH·), nitric oxide (NO·), chlorine (Cl·) and bromine (Br·). In the stratosphere, OH· and NO· come mostly from nature, but human activity has sharply raised chlorine and bromine, carried up inside stable compounds such as CFCs. A chlorine atom is not used up: it is free to repeat its two-step cycle, and on average one atom reacts with about 100,000 ozone molecules before leaving the cycle. Bromine destroys even more ozone per atom, but there is far less of it in the air.

paragraphs.heading: Measuring the hole
paragraphs.text: The ozone hole is usually measured as the drop in total column ozone above a point on Earth's surface, given in Dobson units (DU). Instruments such as the Total Ozone Mapping Spectrometer (TOMS) have shown marked falls in the Antarctic spring and early summer compared with the early 1970s and before. Losses of up to 70 percent in the ozone column over Antarctica in southern spring were first reported in 1985 and are still going on. As of 2010, Antarctic ozone in September and October remained 40–50 percent below pre-hole values.

paragraphs.heading: Signs of recovery
paragraphs.text: Controls on ozone-depleting substances took effect in 1989. By the mid-1990s ozone levels had steadied, and in the 2000s they started to recover. A gradual healing trend was reported in 2016, and in 2019 NASA said the hole was the smallest since its discovery in 1982. The ozone hole had been expected to return to pre-1980 levels by around 2075, but the UN now projects that, under current rules, the layer will fully regenerate by 2045.
